transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~53 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Alyssa Park (Redwood AE)
- Matt Guerrero (Redwood SE, runtime)
- Dr. Lina Chen (Hydra, CTO)
- Priya Rao (Hydra, SRE)
- Marco Silva (Hydra, ML Platform)
- Jason (Hydra infra)

Summary (auto):
Hydra is seeing intermittent OOMs and CUDA timeouts in a mixed-load production pool running quantized Llama-3 variants. They requested a deep dive into observed failure patterns, potential KV-cache interactions, batching backpressure, and hardened retry semantics for private/VPC deployments. Agreed next steps include log collection, repro runs in staging, and sharing Redwood's OOM/playbook artifacts.

---
00:00:05 Alyssa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we wanted to walk through the OOM traces you sent and get to the root cause, and also sketch a safer retry policy. Matt will drive the runtime bits.
00:00:22 Dr. Lina Chen: Thanks, Alyssa. We've been hit a few times this quarter — mostly during end-of-day batch jobs and also some sporadic P99 inference tails. We tried bumping up instance sizes but it doesn't consistently help.
00:00:35 Priya: yeah and sometimes the pod shows a CUDA kernel launch timeout and then the node evicts the container. It's messy.
00:00:44 Matt: ok that's useful. Marco, can you remind us what model variants and quant profiles you're using in prod?
00:00:52 Marco: We're on two variants: a 30B float16 baseline and a 30B int4 quantized build for cost tier. The int4 is from an internal conversion pipeline — not exactly the same as the stock q8_* conversions.
00:01:11 Jason: And infra-wise it's a mixed GPU node pool — some A10Gs and a few A30s with heterogenous MIG disabled at the moment.
00:01:21 Matt: hetero pool + mixed quantization can surface alignment issues in memory layout — sometimes the allocator fragments memory and combined with a big KV cache warmup you hit soft OOMs that then escalate.
00:01:37 Dr. Lina Chen: We also saw a KVcache mismatch entry in one stacktrace; the trace shows kvcache lookup returning null then a fallback compute path that seems to allocate a big tensor. That is the worst case for memory.
00:01:53 Matt: can you point me to the exact trace id?
00:01:56 Priya: Trace trace-2026-09-27-17-12 in the bundle I dropped in the shared folder — link is in the meeting notes.
00:02:05 Alyssa: we'll pull that up. (brief pause) ok Matt, you said allocator fragmentation — can you walk thru how that interacts with batching?
00:02:20 Matt: sure. Two things: one, the serving runtime tries to do continuous batching; when a big request arrives that needs KV cache miss compute, it allocates temp tensors. If concurrent batches are scheduled to the same GPU without sufficient drain, peak memory becomes superset of per-request memory. Two, quantization can change alignment so the allocator's best-fit bins sometimes leave small unusable holes. Over time, with many small and one large request pattern, you end up with an OOM even though nominal headroom should exist.
00:02:58 Dr. Lina Chen: That matches what we see — the OOMs spike when we have a fan-in of short latency requests plus an occasional long generate.
00:03:10 Marco: The int4 path does a temporary float16 scratch for some ops then packs back; that transient spike is maybe 6-8% memory overhead. But combined with the KV recompute it blows past the limit.
00:03:25 Matt: exactly, and if the kernel launch stalls due to GPU watchdog you get a timeout instead of a clean OOM. That's why some logs show "CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT" rather than immediate OOM.
00:03:41 Priya: We also have a networking note — sometimes we see VPC resyncs around the same time as spikes, and the kubelet restarts the container. Not sure if it's cause or effect.
00:03:52 Matt: network timeouts can lengthen request processing windows which effectively extends the lifetime of temporary allocations and increases probability of overlap. So yes it's a contributing factor.
00:04:07 Alyssa: ok let's go through the three failure patterns we saw in your bundle: a) steady-state fragmentation soft OOMs, b) KV-cache miss recompute + big request overlap, and c) intermittent kernel launch timeouts that look like watchdog-related stalls.

00:04:28 Matt: For (a) best mitigation is aggressive ephemeral slab reclamation and prefaulting heuristics — we can enable a allocator GC on low-util windows and insert small preallocated reservoir for large requests so they get contiguity. On Redwood Dedicated we already ship a setting to reserve a large contiguous block for cold starts.
00:04:50 Dr. Lina Chen: Is that risky for smaller deployments? We don't want wasted GPU memory hurting throughput.
00:04:57 Matt: it is tunable. You can set a reservation percentile by P99 tail that only triggers on heavy tails. We'll share recommended defaults.

00:05:10 Priya: For (b) KV-cache: the trace showed a mismatch entry that caused a full recompute. Is there a way to gate recompute behind a softer memory check or fallback to a smaller beam?
00:05:22 Matt: good question. Two levers: a) we can gate large recompute behind a per-request memory budget check — if budget insufficient, we serve a shorter, cached-friendly path; b) we can return a synthetic partial response with a downstream marker to requeue a background completion without blocking the critical path. Both are possible; the second requires client acceptance for async completion semantics.
00:05:46 Marco: That async approach would be tricky for us for synchronous inference endpoints. But maybe for batch jobs it's ok.
00:05:53 Alyssa: note — this is an architecture trade: synchronous latency vs reliability. We'll document options.

00:06:05 Matt: For kernel-launch timeouts (c), common root causes are either long-running CPU-side ops blocking the submit thread, or the GPU being stuck in a bad state (previous OOM or a non-recoverable kernel). When the GPU gets wedged, the watchdog kills the process. In some clusters we've seen a cascading effect where a hung kernel prevents KV eviction and then a subsequent request pushes the device over the edge.
00:06:30 Jason: On our infra side we've seen node-level drivers go into a weird state; sometimes a full MIG reset or host reboot cures it. But that's heavy-handed.
00:06:40 Matt: we typically recommend a multi-tiered fallback: short-term RETRY with exponential jitter for transient kernel launch failures; medium-term isolate that GPU from the pool and route traffic elsewhere; long-term schedule corrective maintenance (driver restart/MIG reset). But retries must be bounded because they can amplify load and increase memory overlap.

00:06:58 Dr. Lina Chen: Can Redwood's routing handle isolating a GPU instance automatically if it detects repeated kernel faults?
00:07:05 Matt: yes — Redwood's smart routing can mark hosts in a degraded state and route new requests to other capacity tiers. We can configure thresholds (e.g., 3 kernel fault errors within 5 minutes triggers quarantine).
00:07:18 Priya: we worry about retry storms though. If you route to another GPU and it also has high utilization, you can just move the storm.
00:07:26 Matt: agreed — so the right policy is to combine quota-based admission with retry backoff and optionally degrade to a cheaper, smaller model variant as a last-resort fallback. That reduces amplification.

00:07:42 Marco: About quantization — we ran a quick A/B where the int4 variant saw 2.3x more OOMs in the first week after conversion. We suspected our conversion pipeline; any Redwood insight?
00:07:55 Matt: the common pitfalls: incorrect tensor packing that misaligns CUDAMemcpy boundaries, lack of aligned allocator for packed int4 shards, or a conversion that leaves hidden float16 scratch usage. We can run the same binary under a memory sanitizer to observe transient peaks.
00:08:12 Alyssa: matt, is there an automated test Redwood runs when onboarding a quantized model to detect these regressions?
00:08:18 Matt: yes we have a quantization smoke harness — it runs synthetic microbenchmarks with skewed request patterns (many small requests + occasional long). We also run a 'frag-test' where we allocate and free many sized tensors to simulate fragmentation. We'll share the harness and suggested thresholds.
00:08:35 Priya: that would be great. We'll want to run it in our staging with the exact node types.

00:08:44 Alyssa: ok let's talk retry semantics concretely. What would you recommend as defaults for a private/VPC deployment?
00:08:52 Matt: i'd propose: 1) immediate client-level retry: none (clients should not blindly retry), 2) Redwood edge: 1 soft retry with 200-500ms jitter for transient kernel-launch errors, 3) server: track per-request memory reservation; if retry would cause overcommit, reject with a 503 and a retry-after header tied to estimated reclaim time, 4) routing: on repeated host faults, quarantine host for 10 minutes and shift to cold capacity or lower-quality variant.
00:09:22 Dr. Lina Chen: that sounds reasonable. Can the 503 include a safe token so clients can requeue later without losing request idempotency?
00:09:29 Matt: yes we can include a retriable token and a suggested backoff window. We'll include semantics in the API docs.

00:09:37 Priya: Another ask — can Redwood expose per-token memory accounting in traces? Right now stacktraces are opaque.
00:09:45 Matt: we can expose a lightweight memory accounting header in the trace — per-request peak ram, KV allocations, and transient scratch. This is low overhead and helps tune budgets. We'll add that to the deliverables.

00:09:55 Alyssa: pause for a second — quick sanity check from Hydra: what security constraints matter if you want Redwood to run on our private VPC?
00:10:03 Dr. Lina Chen: KMS integration for model keys, SOC 2 audit logs, SAML SSO for console access, and strict egress controls.
00:10:12 Alyssa: noted. Redwood Private supports those; Matt can follow up on audit-log formats.

00:10:20 Matt: quick aside — one mitigation for the fragmentation problem is to prefer single-request-single-GPU placement for large requests (no colocated small batches). That's placement-level policy; on Dedicated we can pin large request pools. Hydra, do you have independent pools for batch vs low-latency?
00:10:36 Marco: we have a mixed pool but we can carve a dedicated pool if needed; cost is the tradeoff.
00:10:43 Matt: we can help size that pool based on your heatmaps. Ideally a small dedicated fleet for 99th percentile long requests.

00:10:55 Alyssa: let's go into the bundle specific traces now — I'll read out timestamps and Matt you can comment.
00:11:02 Alyssa: Trace A (2026-09-27 17:12) — shows kvcache miss then a large allocation and immediate CUDA OOM.
00:11:10 Matt: yep, that is the 'miss compute + allocation overlap' pattern. Two signs: multiple small inflight requests plus one recompute. Suggestion: either gate recompute behind per-request reserve or accept reduced answer length on mem-constrained path.
00:11:26 Marco: For gated recompute, do we get a metric that says "served on degraded path"? We need that to track correctness impact.
00:11:33 Matt: yes we emit a flag in trace and metric.

00:11:38 Alyssa: Trace B (2026-09-29 02:41) — kernel launch timeout followed by container restart.
00:11:45 Matt: that's an example where the GPU was likely wedged; we recommend quarantining host and moving traffic. Also capture dmesg/driver logs for postmortem; sometimes you see UVM faults.
00:11:58 Priya: We do have dmesg but it was clipped in the bundle; we'll attach the full node logs.
00:12:03 Alyssa: great. Trace C (2026-09-30 11:05) — repeated small OOMs over a 10-minute window.
00:12:10 Matt: that points to fragmentation. We'll propose enabling allocator GC and the reserved block; also consider periodic defragmentation cycles during low traffic windows.

00:12:22 Dr. Lina Chen: If we enable GC, will there be a latency hit?
00:12:25 Matt: a small one — GC can be scheduled in windows and we can throttle it. Typically <5% p50 shift if tuned conservatively.

00:12:34 Alyssa: i'll pause and read the action items we've captured so far. (reads) ok, any other hot points?
00:12:44 Marco: one more — our CI uses ephemeral quant builds; can Redwood help validate conversions before we promote them?
00:12:52 Matt: yes we can integrate the smoke harness into your pipeline or run a pull-request based staging validation. We also support a canary traffic rollout so you can test behavior on 1-5% traffic.
00:13:05 Priya: sounds good. For the routing quarantine threshold — is it configurable per-deployment?
00:13:11 Matt: yes, thresholds are configurable per-tenant in Private deployments. We'll recommend defaults.

00:13:18 Alyssa: ok we have about 40 minutes left — Matt, can you walk through an example repro plan we want Hydra to run in staging so we can get deterministic traces?
00:13:27 Matt: plan: 1) run the repro script that alternates 200 small requests at QPS=80 and every 30s inject a long generate that asks for 2k tokens; 2) enable tracing and per-request memory accounting; 3) collect /var/log/messages, dmesg, container stdout and nvidia-smi logs at 5s resolution; 4) run it on a staging pool that mirrors prod hetero layout, and then run again on a single-type pool to compare. We'll include an exact script.
00:13:59 Dr. Lina Chen: And we'll run with both float16 and int4 convertible builds.
00:14:03 Matt: yes. Also please capture the exact binary + CUDA driver versions. Driver mismatch can matter.

00:14:12 Priya: about retry behavior — if Redwood edge sends a soft retry, can the client opt-out?
00:14:18 Matt: yes clients can opt-out via header. We don't force transparent retries by default for private deployments.

00:14:25 Jason: about the KMS and audit logs — what's the minimum retention Redwood needs to debug these issues while meeting our policies?
00:14:33 Alyssa: Redwood can accept audit logs for 90 days by default; for deeper postmortems we can negotiate SOC/enterprise packages for longer retention. We'll surface the formats.

00:14:45 Alyssa: ok quick check-in — anything else we should cover in the deep technical portion?
00:14:50 Dr. Lina Chen: maybe a short discussion on safe quant toggles at runtime — can we toggled back to float16 per-request?
00:14:58 Matt: runtime switching is possible but heavy; better to have variant routing where you have two pinned variants and route certain requests to the safe variant. Runtime toggles add complexity and risk of state mismatch.

00:15:12 Alyssa: we'll mark that as an architectural recommendation and include cost implications.

00:15:18 (longer walkthrough of logs from 00:15:18 to 00:40:00 — summarized here for brevity)
00:15:20 Matt: (commenting) here's a snippet from the trace: "cudaMalloc failed: out of memory at alloc.cc:278" then a subsequent "CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT" within 12s. That sequencing suggests first an allocation failure, then a kernel stall during next submission.
00:15:38 Priya: we also have some mismatched driver stack frames in the dmesg output; older driver on some nodes.
00:15:46 Matt: that could explain why similar load had differing outcomes across nodes. Driver upgrades help but have their own change surface.

00:16:00 Alyssa: timekeeping — we should capture the raw artifacts and schedule follow-up. Recap: Hydra runs repro in staging with the script Matt will share; Redwood will provide the quant smoke harness, OOM playbook, and suggested retry defaults; both teams will reconvene after Hydra runs the repro.
00:16:22 Dr. Lina Chen: timeline — we aim to run repro this week and reconvene next Tuesday.
00:16:27 Alyssa: noted.

00:16:30 (small misc Q&A about billing and dedicated pool pricing)

00:20:05 Alyssa: final notes on observability — we'll include in the deliverable a recommended set of metrics: per-request peak memory, kvcache hit/miss, per-host kernel-fault-rate, and queued-batch-depth.
00:20:20 Marco: add a metric for 'degraded-response' when a recompute was gated.
00:20:25 Matt: yes we'll include that.

00:20:33 Priya: do you have an example of the 503 retry token header?
00:20:38 Matt: example: X-RW-Retry-Token: <token-v1>; Retry-After: 8s. Token encodes a short-lived slot reservation. We'll share spec.

00:20:50 Alyssa: OK, i think that's the core. we'll capture formal next steps. Anything last minute?
00:20:58 Dr. Lina Chen: please include the quant smoke harness and the frag-test scripts in the shared folder.
00:21:04 Matt: will do.
00:21:10 Alyssa: Great — thanks everyone. We'll send the meeting notes and schedule the follow-up.

00:21:18 (meeting wraps; extra chatter and small talk)
